I have launched Nexhub as a beta Today. And wanted to share what it meant to me.

Here is the beta. Please contact me using Gmail/Medium for Access if you wish to see/use it.

Thank you for reading my first post, I will be back with more.

medium.titulo: Stop Wasting Tokens: 15 Claude Code Techniques Every Developer Should Know
medium.resumo: Practical habits that cut your usage, speed up your sessions, and get better code out of Claude.
medium.conteudo_html:
Practical habits that cut your usage, speed up your sessions, and get better code out of Claude.

If you’ve used Claude Code for more than a week, you’ve probably hit one of these moments: a session that suddenly feels sluggish, answers that start forgetting decisions you made an hour ago, or a usage limit that arrives far sooner than you expected.

Almost every one of these problems has the same root cause: context. Every message you send carries the conversation so far with it: your CLAUDE.md, tool definitions, every file Claude has read, every test log it has scrolled through. The bigger that pile gets, the more each turn costs, and the harder it becomes for the model to focus on what actually matters.

The good news is that managing context is a skill, and a learnable one. Here are 15 techniques I use daily to keep Claude Code fast, focused, and cheap.

1. Keep your CLAUDE.md lean

CLAUDE.md is loaded into every single session, which makes it the most expensive text in your project. Treat it like a README for a very smart new teammate: build and test commands, key conventions, and the few gotchas that bite everyone.

What doesn’t belong there: full API docs, long style guides, or a history of every decision. Link to those files instead, and Claude can read them when a task actually needs them. If your CLAUDE.md has grown past a couple of screens, it’s time to prune.

2. Use /clear between unrelated tasks

Finished fixing the login bug and now want to work on the billing page? Run /clear. Carrying the whole auth investigation into a billing task wastes tokens on every turn and can quietly steer Claude toward the wrong files.

A good rule of thumb: one task, one session.

3. Compact with intent, not by accident

When a long task genuinely needs its history, use /compact to summarize the conversation and free up space. Better still, tell it what to keep:

/compact Keep the database schema decisions and the list of failing tests. Drop the exploration.

Compacting on your own terms, at a natural break point, beats waiting for auto-compaction to kick in mid-thought.

4. Look at what’s filling your context with /context

You can’t optimize what you can’t see. /context shows a breakdown of what's occupying the window: system prompt, tools, MCP servers, memory files, and conversation. The first time you run it, you'll often find a surprise, like an MCP server you forgot about quietly eating a big chunk of space before you've typed a word.

5. Point directly at files with @ mentions

“Fix the validation bug in the signup form” sends Claude on a search: listing directories, grepping, opening candidates. Every one of those steps costs tokens.

“Fix the email validation in @src/components/SignupForm.tsx" skips the hunt entirely. If you already know where the code lives, say so.

6. Write specific prompts

Vague prompts lead to exploration, guesses, and rework, which is the most expensive loop of all. A good prompt names:

  • Where: the file, function, or module
  • What: the expected behavior, ideally with an example
  • Constraints: “don’t add dependencies”, “keep the public API unchanged”
  • Done: how you’ll know it worked, such as a test that should pass

Thirty extra seconds of typing routinely saves thousands of tokens of back-and-forth.

7. Plan before you build

For anything larger than a small fix, switch to plan mode (Shift+Tab) and ask Claude to propose an approach before touching code. Reviewing a ten-line plan is cheap. Discovering the wrong approach after 400 lines have been written across six files is not.

8. Delegate exploration to subagents

Questions like “how is authentication wired through this codebase?” can involve reading dozens of files. Ask Claude to use a subagent for that investigation. The subagent does the reading in its own separate context and hands back only a summary, so your main session stays clean and focused on the actual change.

9. Trim your MCP servers

Every connected MCP server contributes tool definitions to your context. Five servers you rarely use can add up to a significant overhead on every request. Use /mcp to review what's connected, and configure servers per project rather than globally so each repo loads only the tools it actually needs.

10. Keep noisy files out of reach

Build output, lockfiles, vendored code, and generated files are rarely useful to read and very expensive when they are. Add deny rules to .claude/settings.json so Claude doesn't wander into them:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Read(./node_modules/**)",
      "Read(./dist/**)",
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./package-lock.json)"
    ]
  }
}

Bonus: this also keeps secrets like .env out of the conversation.

11. Pick the right model for the job

You don’t need the most powerful model to rename a variable or write a docstring. Use /model to switch: a lighter, faster model for routine edits and boilerplate, the heavyweight for architecture, gnarly debugging, and tricky refactors. Matching the model to the task is one of the simplest cost levers you have.

12. Interrupt early, and rewind instead of arguing

If Claude heads in the wrong direction, press Esc right away. Don’t wait for it to finish a doomed approach.

And when a change goes badly, resist the urge to pile on corrections (“no, not like that… undo that part… actually go back…”). Each correction adds more noise to the context. Use /rewind (or press Esc twice) to jump back to a checkpoint, then re-prompt with a clearer instruction.

13. Tame command output

A full test suite run or a verbose build can dump thousands of lines into context in one go. Ask for less:

  • Run a single test file instead of the whole suite
  • Use quiet flags like --silent, -q, or --reporter=dot
  • Pipe long output through tail -50 or grep -i error

Put your preferred “quiet” commands in CLAUDE.md so Claude uses them by default.

14. Turn repeated workflows into skills and slash commands

If you find yourself pasting the same long instructions (“here’s how we write migrations”, “here’s our release checklist”), package them as a custom slash command or a skill. Skills are especially efficient: only a short description sits in context until the skill is actually needed, and then the full instructions load on demand.

15. Go headless for one-shot jobs

Not every task needs an interactive session. For scripted or repeatable jobs, like generating a changelog, triaging lint errors, or summarizing a diff in CI, use headless mode:

claude -p "Summarize the changes in this diff for release notes" < changes.diff

Each run starts fresh with exactly the context it needs, and nothing accumulates. When you do need to pick up yesterday’s work, use --continue or --resume deliberately rather than keeping one giant session alive for days.

Quick cheat sheet

  • Before a session: lean CLAUDE.md, only the MCP servers you need, deny rules for noisy files
  • During a session: @ mentions, specific prompts, plan mode, subagents, quiet commands, the right model
  • When things drift: Esc, /rewind, /compact with instructions
  • Between tasks: /clear
  • For automation: skills, slash commands, and claude -p

Final thought

Saving tokens isn’t really about being stingy. A focused context produces sharper answers, fewer hallucinated file paths, and faster responses. The habits that keep your bill down are the same habits that make Claude Code a better collaborator.

Start with two or three of these this week. My suggestion: /clear between tasks, @ mentions for files, and a quick look at /context. You'll feel the difference within a day.

Which of these techniques do you already use, and which one surprised you? Let me know in the comments.

Build truly native mobile apps with Vue and the Nuxt developer experience, powered by NativeScript.

Today, we’re introducing the developer preview of Nuxt Native — an open-source framework for building native mobile applications using Vue and familiar Nuxt conventions.

If you already love building with Nuxt, Nuxt Native aims to make mobile development feel familiar too.

Instead of rendering your application inside a WebView, Nuxt Native uses NativeScript to render real native UI on Android and iOS.

With Nuxt Native, we’re bringing familiar ideas from the Nuxt ecosystem to native development:

  • Vue Single File Components
  • File-based routing
  • Nuxt-style composables
  • Native UI components
  • Pinia support
  • Native device APIs
  • Simple CLI and developer tooling

This is just the beginning.

Repo:

https://github.com/vastx-tech/nuxt-native

Nuxt Native is currently in Developer Preview, and there is still a lot to build, improve, and explore. We’re releasing early so developers can try it, experiment with it, contribute, and help shape its future.

Our goal is simple:

Make native mobile development feel natural for Vue and Nuxt developers.

Welcome to Nuxt Native. 🚀

medium.titulo: SPA (React/Vue) vs. htmx: Why Towami Chose a Document-First Frontend
medium.resumo: A marketplace page should arrive as usable HTML — for search engines, modern laptops, and mid-range phones on mobile networks.
medium.conteudo_html:
A marketplace page should arrive as usable HTML — for search engines, modern laptops, and mid-range phones on mobile networks.

React and Vue are excellent tools. We chose a different architecture for Towami’s public catalog and merchant storefronts because of the product’s requirements, not because JavaScript frameworks are inherently slow or bad for SEO.

Where React and Vue are the right choice

When the product is primarily an application — a design tool, trading terminal, collaborative editor, or state-heavy dashboard — a component framework and client runtime are often the most productive choice.

The ecosystems are mature, the development model is widely understood, and frameworks such as Next.js and Nuxt can return fully rendered HTML from the server. A React or Vue application is not automatically a client-only SPA, nor is it automatically bad for search.

Shopify illustrates why the distinction matters. Its standard theme stack is an excellent default for many merchants, with mature commerce tooling and broad app compatibility. Shopify Markets supports localized languages, currencies, pricing, and domains. For teams that need a custom headless storefront and already work in React, Hydrogen is also a strong option.

Those are rational choices. Towami’s requirements simply led to a different trade-off.

The boundary we have

Towami has two closely connected public surfaces:

  • country marketplaces across nine markets, with localized English and Spanish routes;
  • white-label merchant storefronts, including storefronts on merchants’ own domains.

Organic search is an important acquisition channel. That means some filter combinations are more than temporary UI state: when they have live inventory, they become indexable landing pages.

For example:

https://cr.towami.com/en/vehicles/cars/for-sale/sedan

That URL needs to return a complete document with a canonical URL, structured data, localized metadata, and — when the combination is eligible — a sitemap entry. It should not exist only after a client-side router has started.

A client-heavy architecture could meet those requirements. But it would add another layer that must remain consistent with the server: routes, locales, currencies, canonical rules, cache variants, and the initial document received by crawlers.

We decided that Towami did not need that layer on its public surfaces.

What the browser receives

Towami’s public UI is rendered by Go using Templ templates.

Browser-side behavior uses htmx, Alpine.js, and a project-specific JavaScript bundle:

  • htmx requests and replaces HTML fragments;
  • Alpine manages local state such as mobile menus, confirmation dialogs, galleries, and checkout options;
  • the site bundle handles behavior that does not fit cleanly into either library.

Navigation is boosted at the <body> level. Ordinary internal links can replace #main-content and update browser history without replacing the entire document. The header remains mounted, with out-of-band updates where its content needs to change.

The initial catalog content arrives as server-rendered HTML. There is no React or Vue hydration step. After an htmx update, Alpine initializes behavior on the new DOM.

Critical CSS for public pages is inlined, while the remaining styles are loaded from separate bundles. Account pages use linked stylesheets because their first render is not an organic-search landing surface.

The largest browser-side dependency is TipTap. It is loaded only in merchant content editors — for products, pages, blog posts, and categories — not in the public catalog.

One URL, two navigation modes

Catalog filters are where this architecture becomes especially useful.

Suppose a visitor selects “sedan.” The filter form uses GET.

For an htmx request, the server:

  1. returns 200 OK;
  2. renders the catalog fragment;
  3. sends HX-Push-Url with the preferred path.

The list updates and the address bar becomes:

/en/vehicles/cars/for-sale/sedan

For an ordinary request — including a browser without JavaScript — the same query-string URL receives a 302 redirect to the preferred path.

There is no crawler detection. The server only distinguishes an htmx request from a regular HTTP request.

Canonical URLs remove non-SEO filters such as price ranges. One allowlisted feature can become the final path segment; additional features remain in ?features=. Sitemap generation only publishes combinations supported by live catalog data.

This gives enhanced navigation to browsers that support it while keeping the underlying links and forms functional without JavaScript.

Keeping response variants separate

A full document and an htmx fragment can share a URL while containing different HTML. The cache must not confuse them.

Towami’s primary full-page and htmx navigation responses use a weak ETag calculated from the rendered body and return:

Vary: Accept, HX-Request, X-Catalog-More
Cache-Control: private, no-cache, must-revalidate

Because the full document, navigation fragment, and “show more” fragment have different bodies, they receive different ETags. A matching conditional request returns 304 Not Modified.

We do not attach a public millisecond claim to this mechanism. The relevant architectural property is simpler: the first response contains the page, while enhanced navigation uses the same URL model instead of creating a second client-only route space.

What we gave up

This approach has costs.

We gave up the standardized React/Vue client-component ecosystem, shared frontend language across server and browser, and the tooling built around large client-side applications.

The merchant interface is also server-rendered. Initial requests return complete Templ pages; subsequent navigation can replace #main-content with htmx fragments. A server-backed interaction usually means implementing a handler that returns markup rather than designing a JSON API and client store.

That model is less attractive for dense interfaces with extensive client state.

We also do not try to turn every transition into app-style navigation. Authentication links and several other flows deliberately perform normal document navigation. Progressive enhancement is a default, not a requirement that every request must be asynchronous.

When we would choose React or Vue

We would choose a client framework if Towami’s primary interface became a real-time operations console, visual page builder, collaborative editor, or another product where most meaningful state lives in the browser.

That would justify the runtime and client-side state model. The public catalog and merchant storefront could still remain document-first.

Modern React and Vue frameworks can also reduce client cost through server components, selective hydration, lazy hydration, and hybrid rendering. The trade-off is therefore one of degree, not an absolute limitation of those technologies.

For Towami, the remaining client-side requirements were small enough that adopting a full application runtime for every public page did not provide enough value.

Performance is a target, not a slogan

Core Web Vitals are among the signals used by Google’s ranking systems, although good scores do not guarantee rankings. Across ecommerce, faster experiences often correlate with better conversion — but that is something each product should measure, not promise in advance.

Towami’s engineering target is a high PageSpeed score and good Core Web Vitals on merchant storefronts. It is not an unconditional guarantee for every page or every uploaded image.

The architecture makes that target more achievable:

  • compiled server-side templates;
  • usable HTML in the initial response;
  • inlined critical CSS;
  • limited JavaScript on public pages;
  • no application-framework hydration;
  • one URL model for visitors and crawlers.

React and Vue remain excellent choices for products that behave primarily as applications. Towami’s public catalog is document-first, with interactivity added where it provides clear value.

corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sábado | 26 de setembro de 2026

Amanhã é dia de Maratona de Berlim, uma das principais provas do calendário mundial, mas com ausências de peso. Sebastian Sawe, um dos únicos homens a correr a maratona oficialmente abaixo de 2 horas, está lesionado e não participa. Kenenisa Bekele, outro nome forte, também está fora por uma lesão no tendão calcâneo. Com isso, a disputa pelo pódio masculino fica mais aberta.

Os atletas mais rápidos na lista de favoritos são o tanzaniano Gabriel Geay (2h03m00s) e os etíopes Getaneh Molla (2h03m34s) e Guye Adola (2h03m46s), embora seus melhores tempos já tenham alguns anos. Entre os que estão em melhor forma recente, destacam-se Shura Kitata (2h03m59s), Dejene Hailu (2h04m15s) e o queniano Erick Sang (2h04m30s). O brasileiro Paulo Paula também está na elite A, com seu tempo de 2h09m51s feito em Sevilha. No feminino, a grande expectativa está sobre a etíope Tigist Assefa, que tentará unificar os recordes mundiais da maratona (prova mista e prova exclusivamente feminina), buscando um tempo abaixo de 2h10m. Ela enfrenta a queniana Rosemary Wanjiru, vencedora da prova no ano passado, que tem como melhor marca 2h16m14s.

O Brasil é o quarto país com o maior número de inscritos na prova, com 1.888 corredores, ficando atrás apenas da Alemanha (21.552), Estados Unidos (7.691) e Grã-Bretanha (3.264).

A premiação para o primeiro colocado (masculino e feminino) é de 30 mil euros. Há bônus por tempo, como 30 mil euros para homens que correrem abaixo de 2h02m e mulheres abaixo de 2h15m. Quem quebrar o recorde mundial leva um bônus adicional de 50 mil euros.

Como assistir à Maratona de Berlim

A transmissão da Maratona de Berlim será feita pela ESPN 2 e pelo aplicativo Disney+, a partir das 3h45 da manhã (horário de Brasília).

Inscrições abertas para a Ultra BM

A Ultra BM, uma das provas mais tradicionais do litoral paulista, já está com inscrições abertas para a edição de 2026. O evento, que acontece no dia 17 de outubro, oferece percursos de 75 km (solo ou revezamento em trio, sexteto e octeto) e 42 km. A prova larga de Bertioga e termina em Bora Bora. Se você quer garantir sua vaga, use o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 para ter um desconto especial. Clique aqui para se inscrever.

Skechers lança o supertênis Aero Elite

A Skechers anunciou o lançamento do seu novo supertênis, o Aero Elite. O modelo promete ser a grande aposta da marca no segmento de alta performance. Pelas primeiras imagens divulgadas, o tênis apresenta um novo design para a placa de carbono e utiliza a espuma Hyper Burst Pro. O visual é moderno e parece ser um tênis bem competitivo, indicando que, desta vez, a Skechers entrou para valer na briga dos supertênis.

Dez Milhas Garoto com transmissão ao vivo

Neste domingo também acontece a 10 Milhas Garoto, uma das corridas mais tradicionais do Brasil. A prova de 16 km, que sai de Vitória e chega em frente à fábrica da Garoto, em Vila Velha, terá transmissão ao vivo. Você poderá acompanhar a partir das 6h20 no canal do YouTube “YESCOM Entretenimento” e também pelo aplicativo Bandplay.

Tudo pronto para a Maratona de Salvador

Eu, Sérgio Rocha, estou em Salvador para correr a maratona de 42 km neste domingo. A prova, que faz parte do Circuito Brasil Gigante, terá largada bem cedo, às 4h40 da manhã, para fugir do calor. A expo da prova ainda está acontecendo hoje, então se você estiver por aqui, passe no estande do Brasil Gigante para trocarmos uma ideia, pegar sua pulseirinha e carimbar seu número de peito com o selo do circuito.

O rock baiano mais tocado

E a resposta para o quiz de ontem: o rock baiano mais tocado no Spotify é “Equalize”, da Pitty. A música acumula impressionantes 184 milhões de reproduções na plataforma.
